summary: Dinosaurs Around the World (ages 7–9): dinosaur fossils have been found on all seven continents, including Antarctica, showing dinosaurs were a global phenomenon. The same kinds of dinosaur (and plants like Glossopteris) found on continents now separated by oceans hint that the land was once joined (Pangaea/Gondwana) and has slowly drifted apart. Learners map famous finds to places on a world map, meet the surprising Antarctica case, and reassemble the joined landmass to see why the same creature appears on now-distant continents. Keep continental drift qualitative ('the land slowly moved').
misconceptions: 'Dinosaurs only lived in a few hot places' — fossils are found on all seven continents, including Antarctica.
'Antarctica never had dinosaurs because it's frozen' — it was once warm and forested; ice now hides most fossils.
'The same dinosaur on two continents means it swam across the ocean' — the continents were joined then and have since drifted apart.
'Fewer fossils in Antarctica means fewer dinosaurs lived there' — it mostly reflects how hard they are to find under ice.
'Continents have always been where they are now' — land masses move slowly over millions of years.

activities.title: Map the finds: dinosaurs lived everywhere
steps: Work with a world map and place or reveal find-pins for famous dinosaurs, one or more on every continent: T. rex (North America), Argentinosaurus (Argentina, South America), Iguanodon (England and Belgium, Europe), Spinosaurus (Egypt and Morocco, Africa), Velociraptor (Mongolia, Asia), Muttaburrasaurus (Australia) and Cryolophosaurus (Antarctica).
For each pin, say the dinosaur's name and the continent/place it was found in.
Count the continents represented and state out loud that fossils have been found on all seven, including Antarctica.
Use a shading or density layer to notice where most finds come from (North America, China, Argentina) versus the sparse Antarctica.
activities.insight: Dinosaurs were not a local curiosity confined to a few hot places — they lived across the whole planet, and fossils of them have been found on every continent.

activities.title: The Antarctica surprise: fewer finds is not fewer dinosaurs
steps: Compare a 'then vs now' picture of Antarctica: once warm and forested → today an ice sheet.
Explain why Antarctica has the fewest dinosaur finds: ice now covers most of the rock, making fossils very hard to find.
Decide whether 'fewer fossils found in Antarctica' means 'fewer dinosaurs lived there', and explain your reasoning.
State that Cryolophosaurus lived in Antarctica back when it was warm and forested.
activities.insight: Antarctica was once warm and forested and had dinosaurs; the few fossils found there reflect how hard they are to find under ice, not a lack of dinosaurs — an 'absence of evidence is not evidence of absence' nuance.

activities.title: Reassemble the land: why the same dinosaur appears oceans apart
steps: Start from today's continents and slide/drag them back together so they fit like a jigsaw into one giant landmass (Pangaea/Gondwana).
Line up a shared dinosaur or plant (e.g. Glossopteris) so it sits across a seam where two continents once joined.
Explain in your own words how the same kind of dinosaur ended up on two continents now separated by a huge ocean (e.g. Africa and South America).
Contrast two explanations: 'the dinosaur swam across the ocean' versus 'the land was joined then and has since drifted apart' — and say which the fossil pattern supports.
activities.insight: Matching dinosaurs and plants on now-distant continents are evidence the land was once joined and has slowly drifted apart over millions of years; the dinosaur walked across land that later split, rather than crossing an ocean.

activities.title: Check and explain (matching plus reasoning)
steps: Match each dinosaur to the continent where it was found (e.g. T. rex → North America, Velociraptor → Asia (found in Mongolia), Argentinosaurus → South America (found in Argentina), Cryolophosaurus → Antarctica).
Answer: which continent, surprisingly, also has dinosaur fossils? (Antarctica.)

Respond to the diagnostic prompt in writing or speech: 'The same kind of dinosaur fossil has been found in both Africa and South America, which today are separated by a huge ocean. How could the same dinosaur have lived on two continents so far apart? Explain your thinking.'

Tackle the deeper prompts: 'Antarctica is frozen today, yet dinosaur fossils are found there — what does that tell you about the past?' and 'If the continents were all joined, why don't we find exactly the same dinosaurs everywhere?'
activities.insight: Learners can recall the global distribution AND construct an explanation for matching fossils, distinguishing 'the animals crossed the ocean' from 'the land was joined and drifted apart.'

checkQuestion: The same kind of dinosaur fossil has been found in both Africa and South America, which today are separated by a huge ocean. How could the same dinosaur have lived on two continents so far apart? Explain your thinking.
checkAnswer: Long ago the continents were joined together as one big landmass, so the dinosaur could walk across land that later split apart. Over millions of years the land drifted to where the continents are now, leaving the same fossils on both sides of the ocean.
